Subject: Clarify: streaming SLA commitments for POC

Hi Aisha,

Hope you're well. We're ramping the Aurora chatbot POC and we're trying to line up expectations for production SLAs as we move past the pilot. Two specifics the security and platform teams asked us to confirm: 1) Time-to-first-token (TTFT) expectations for streaming endpoints vs non-streaming (synchronous) endpoints, and 2) sustained token/sec guarantees (or guidance) under normal reserved capacity versus burst behavior.

We saw the public SLOs but there are a few gray areas for regulated workloads: if we have long system prompts (10k tokens) and use streaming, what TTFT should we lock into for our contract amendment? Also, when workload has a sustained throughput (avg 50 tokens/sec per connection across 200 concurrent connections), what should we assume for steady-state per-tenant throughput and for throttling behavior?

Platform team would like a written carve-out they can take to procurement/security. Can you point me to the right contact or propose wording we can use? We need to share something with procurement by end of next week.

Thanks,
Tim
Timothy Lewis
Director, Platform Engineering

Aisha — quick technical note and a proposed carve-out draft below. High-level: streaming TTFT is influenced by two factors we own (scheduling and model init/KV priming) and one the client controls (request serialization and local network). For long system prompts the dominant cost is model tokenization + KV cache load — that's warm path.

Definitions to use in legal wording (suggested):
- "Time-to-First-Token (TTFT)": elapsed time from Redwood's receipt of a valid streaming request to the delivery of the first payload byte to the client's open stream.
- "Sustained Token Rate": average number of output tokens emitted per second measured over any 60s window for a single logical connection.

Proposed measurable commitments (for Dedicated capacity with reserved pool P):
- TTFT (streaming): 95th percentile <= 450 ms for requests with prompt payloads <= 2k tokens and with model cache warm.
- TTFT (streaming): 95th percentile <= 1,200 ms for requests with prompt payloads between 2k-10k tokens (accounts for tokenization and KV warm-up).
- TTFT (sync/non-streaming): 95th percentile <= 2,500 ms for the same prompt classes (sync incurs full response assembly before return).
- Sustained Token Rate per connection: baseline guidance 25-75 tokens/sec depending on model size and quantization; guaranteed floor for Dedicated customers: 20 tokens/sec per connection as long as the tenant's aggregate usage is within their reserved throughput.

Fallbacks/over-cap behavior:
- During transient overloads or when reserved pool limits are reached, Redwood will: 1) signal 429 with backoff hints; 2) optionally reroute to lower-cost quantized variant (if customer opts into fallbacks); 3) apply per-tenant shaping to preserve global SLOs.

SLI/Ops mapping (what we'll measure):
- TTFT measured at ingress gateway to egress stream boundary (ms); breach triggered if 95th% over a daily window exceeds committed threshold.
- Sustained Token Rate measured per connection as the average tokens/sec over a 60s rolling window; alert when average drops below the guaranteed floor for >2 consecutive minutes.

Client-side recommendations to meet TTFT:
- Open persistent streams and reuse them across requests where possible.
- Send large system prompts only once and use KV caching; prefer incremental context updates for frequently changing session state.

Draft contract paragraph (single-paragraph amendment for procurement):
"Redwood Inference will use commercially reasonable efforts to meet the following production commitments for streaming endpoints served from the customer's dedicated capacity pool: 95th percentile Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) not to exceed 450 ms for payloads <=2k tokens when model caches are warm, and not to exceed 1,200 ms for payloads between 2k-10k tokens. For non-streaming (synchronous) endpoints the 95th percentile response time is targeted at 2,500 ms under equivalent conditions. Redwood further guarantees a floor of 20 tokens/second sustained rate per connection while the customer remains within their reserved throughput allocation; Redwood will provide metrics and alerting to demonstrate adherence. In the event of cluster-wide overloads, Redwood may apply per-tenant shaping, reroute to compatible model variants, or return 429 responses with backoff guidance; Redwood will notify the customer and work to remediate capacity constraints."

I've attached a short spreadsheet that maps these commitments to the SLO plumbing (what metrics we record and which alarms fire). I can tighten the numbers further if legal asks for stiffer guarantees but these are what we can reliably measure and defend.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference

Tim — thanks for the clear ask and timeline. Apologies for the multi-day reply; pulled the team together and we have a concise package you can share with procurement/security. See summary and attachments below.

Summary (one paragraph to paste into an amendment):
Redwood Inference will use commercially reasonable efforts to meet the following production commitments for streaming endpoints served from the customer's dedicated capacity pool: 95th percentile Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) not to exceed 450 ms for prompt payloads <=2k tokens when model caches are warm, and not to exceed 1,200 ms for payloads between 2k-10k tokens. For non-streaming (synchronous) endpoints the 95th percentile response time is targeted at 2,500 ms under equivalent conditions. Redwood further guarantees a floor of 20 tokens/second sustained rate per connection while the customer remains within their reserved throughput allocation; Redwood will provide metrics and alerting to demonstrate adherence. During cluster-wide overloads or planned maintenance, Redwood may apply per-tenant shaping, return 429 responses with backoff hints, or reroute to a compatible quantized model variant if previously authorized; Redwood will notify the customer and use commercially reasonable efforts to restore committed performance.

What we've attached:
- initial-frame-slo-proposal.pdf — single-page slide with the commitments and definitions (for procurement)
- slo-metrics-mapping.xlsx — mapping of SLIs, thresholds, and alert playbooks (for Aurora Ops)

Operational notes for Aurora Ops (short):
- Measure TTFT at client egress using the request id we supply; we'll expose the same metric in the tenant dashboard.
- For best TTFT, open persistent streaming sessions and reuse them; avoid sending very large system prompts on every turn.
- If you want guaranteed higher sustained throughput, we can discuss a higher reserved pool commitment (commit more GPUs) or an explicit burst add-on.

Next steps:
1) Confirm this paragraph is acceptable for your procurement/security teams and let us know any redline.
2) If they want stronger numeric guarantees (e.g., lower TTFT ceilings or higher guaranteed tokens/sec), we'll need to capture that as an amendment with clearly defined penalties and an SRE-run capacity assessment — we can scope that work and provide a pricing add-on.
3) I'll push the attached documents into a shared Drive and open a short 30-minute follow-up with your platform lead if helpful.

If this looks good, Monica will coordinate the amendment language with your procurement contacts and Jonas will onboard the SLI dashboards for the POC.

Best,
Aisha
